ta-l1d35q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinctions 35–48. Having treated the procession of the persons in one essence, principle and cause of creatures, Lombard, before treating creatures, treats what makes up the complete character of God as principle. For agents by nature, power suffices, but for voluntary agents knowledge and will are also required (the Philosopher), so he treats God's knowledge (Dist. 35–41), power (Dist. 42–44), and will (Dist. 45–48), in that order because knowledge extends to more than power, covering evils too, and power to more than will, covering infinitely many things God could make. On knowledge he treats it in general and then predestination (Dist. 40); in general, whose knowledge it is and how it relates to the things known (Dist. 38); within the first, that God knows all things and how they are in his knowledge (Dist. 36). Here he shows that God's one, simple wisdom takes various names (knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, providence, predestination) from the states and effects of things, and which of these would hold if there were no creatures. Five articles are announced: whether there is knowledge in God; whether he knows only himself or others; whether he knows them with certain and proper knowledge; whether his knowledge is univocal with ours; and whether it is universal or particular, potential or habitual.
claims: Knowledge, power, and will complete the character of God as voluntary principle.
God's one wisdom is named variously from its objects.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e147.summary: First argument that knowledge does not fit God. Where there is no intellect there is no knowledge, and 'intellect' does not properly fit God, since the Liber de causis says that when God is called intelligent he is named by the name of his first creature, intelligence.
claims: God is named intelligent from his first effect.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e153.summary: Second argument. Nothing fits the simplest and first that presupposes something to which it is added, and knowledge presupposes life and being (Liber de causis).
claims: Knowledge presupposes being and life.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e156.summary: Third argument. Knowledge requires a plurality, of knower, knowledge, and knowable, which does not fit the supremely one.
claims: Knowledge requires plurality.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e160.summary: Fourth argument, against identifying knower and known in God. Nothing is like itself (Hilary) or receives itself, but knowledge is assimilation of knower to known and reception of the knowable in the knower.
claims: Knowledge is assimilation and reception.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e163.summary: Fifth argument. Knowledge (scientia) concerns conclusions and understanding (intellectus) principles (the Philosopher), and knowledge of conclusions follows rational inquiry, which is not in God.
claims: Scientia follows discursive inquiry.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e166.summary: Sed contra from Col. 2:3, 'in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge', and the Commentator (Metaphysics 11), who says life and knowledge are properly in God.
claims: Scripture and the Commentator ascribe knowledge to God.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e172.summary: Second sed contra. The most perfect lacks no perfection, and knowledge is the noblest perfection, so God, in whom the perfections of all genera are united (Metaphysics 5), cannot lack it.
claims: The most perfect has every perfection.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e175.summary: Thomas's determination. According to Dionysius we reach God from creatures by three ways, removal, causality, and eminence, each of which leads to God's knowledge. By removal: since all potency and materiality are removed from God, pure first act, his essence is free of matter and pure form. As matter is the principle of particularity, intelligibility belongs to form, which is the principle of knowledge, so every form existing separate from matter is of intellectual nature: if subsistent, it is intelligent; if not, but a perfection of a subsistent, it is a principle of understanding, as every non-subsistent form is a principle of operation rather than an operator, like heat in fire. God is free of all matter and subsistent, since his being depends on nothing, so he is intelligent and knowing. By causality: every agent intends and desires an end, and every desire of an end is preceded by knowledge setting the end and directing means. In some agents this knowledge is not joined to the agent, which is directed by a prior agent, as an arrow by the archer, as in all natural agents, whose operation is determined by an intellect instituting nature (the work of nature is the work of intelligence); in others, like animals, it is joined. The first cannot act by necessity of nature, or it would be directed by a prior intelligence, so it acts by intellect and will and is knowing. By eminence: what is found more and more in things as they approach something is found most in it, as heat in fire; things nearer the first participate knowledge more nobly, humans more than brutes and angels more than humans, so the noblest knowledge is in God.
claims: God is knowing by the way of removal (immaterial subsistent form), of causality (the first agent directs nature to ends), and of eminence (degrees of knowledge).
Immateriality is the root of knowledge.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e178.summary: Reply to the first argument. When knowledge, intellect, or any perfection is denied of God, it is by excess, not defect (Dionysius: 'without mind and without sense' is to be ordered in God by excess). So 'intellect' is said not to fit God properly because he understands not in a creature's mode but more eminently.
claims: Negations of perfections in God are by excess.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e185.summary: Reply to the second argument. There are three opinions on such names. Some say knowledge, life, and the like signify dispositions added to the essence, which would put composition and potency in God, which is absurd. Others say they predicate only God's being and are said improperly, either by negation ('knowing' = not ignorant like a stone) or by likeness of effect ('angry' because he punishes like an angry man). This is insufficient: every negation is founded on something real, as 'man is not an ass' on human nature, so denying ignorance of God requires positing its opposite in him; and every act proceeds from an agent by something in it, as the hot heats, so in what performs the act of knowledge there must be something belonging to knowledge, though punishing is an act of justice, not of anger. So all such names are said properly of God as to the thing signified, though not as to the mode of signifying, and as to what is proper to each concept, not as to its genus. Whatever implies no material or bodily disposition is truly, and more truly, in God and implies no composition: as these names fit creatures properly because of different things in them, they fit God properly because of his one simple being, which pre-contains the powers of all uniformly (Dionysius). Compare three men each knowing one science (natural philosophy, geometry, grammar) and a fourth who knows all by one habit: he is truly a grammarian, geometer, and philosopher, and though there is one thing in him by which all fit, each name signifies something different in concept, since each imperfectly expresses that thing. So in God, one simple being has the power and perfection of being, living, understanding, and all such, which in creatures are by different things, and each name expresses part of his perfection, not all; so they are one in reality and differ in concept, a concept founded in the truth and perfection of the thing, and as God is properly called being, he is properly called knowing and willing, with no plurality, addition, or order in reality.
claims: Names like 'knowing' are said properly of God as to the thing signified, not as mere negation or likeness of effect.
They are one in reality and conceptually distinct, founded on his one being that pre-contains all perfections, as one habit can contain many sciences.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e188.summary: Reply to the third argument. Knowledge requires knowledge, knower, and known, but not that they differ really, as motion requires mover and moved, though that the moved differs from the mover is known only by demonstration. In every intellect knower and known are in some way the same, in some also in some way different, in some wholly the same. The human intellect, sometimes potential and sometimes actual, when potentially understanding is not the same as the potential intelligible, a thing outside the soul; to understand actually, the potential intelligible must become actually intelligible by its species being stripped of material appendages by the agent intellect, and that species, actually understood, must perfect the potential intellect, and from their union one perfect thing results, the intellect in act, as man results from soul and body. So the actually understood is not other than the actually understanding intellect, though the species does not become the intellect's substance or part except formally. An intellect like the divine, potential to nothing, wholly and always act, does not differ from what it understands in reality but only in consideration: its essence considered as free of matter is understanding; as taken by intellect without matter it is understood; and the understood as not lacking to the understander but in himself is understanding or knowledge, since knowledge is the impression or union of the known with the knower.
claims: Knower and known are one in act; in God, pure act, they differ only conceptually.
God's essence is knower, known, and knowledge under different considerations.
concepts: identity of intellect and intelligible in act

ta-l1d35q1-d1e191.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Terms like assimilation, apprehension, and impression come from considering the possible intellect, which knows only by receiving a species to which it is in potency, by which it is assimilated to the thing outside. Where there is intellect only in act, none of these is said properly, only by our mode of understanding.
claims: Receptive vocabulary belongs to the possible intellect.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e194.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. What is said of God is understood by eminence, removing all imperfection, so the discursus of inquiring reason is removed from God's knowledge and its rectitude about the known retained. Since knowledge properly concerns complexes and understanding the quiddity, God is called knowing as he knows his being and understanding as he knows his nature, which is his being and no simpler, so in God understanding and knowing differ only conceptually. Wisdom is not counted with them, since all wisdom is knowledge but not conversely, only knowledge of the highest causes, by which everything consequent is ordered and known, so God is properly wise as he knows himself, and understanding and knowing as he knows himself and others.
claims: In God knowledge lacks discursus; scientia and intellectus differ only conceptually.
God is wise as knowing himself, the highest cause.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e206.summary: First argument that God does not understand things other than himself. The understood perfects the understander, and every perfection exceeds what it perfects, so if he understood another it would be greater than he.
claims: The understood perfects the understander.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e209.summary: Second argument. The nobility of operations follows that of objects (perfect happiness concerns the noblest object), and everything other than God is baser, so understanding it would debase his operation.
claims: Base objects debase operation.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e212.summary: Third argument. The understood relate to the intellect as pictures to a tablet, and one body cannot bear several figures at once in the same part, so one intellect cannot understand many at once, and God would have succession and weariness.
claims: One intellect cannot understand many at once.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e216.summary: Fourth argument. Sciences are divided as things are, so if God knows many things he has many sciences, implying plurality in his essence, which is his knowledge.
claims: Many objects, many sciences.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e219.summary: Sed contra from Heb. 4:13, 'all things are naked and open to his eyes'.
claims: God sees all things.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e225.summary: Second sed contra. God knows his essence, by which he is principle of things, so he knows himself as principle, and one cannot know something as principle without knowing what it is principle of, since knowing one relative is knowing the other (Categories).
claims: Knowing oneself as cause includes knowing the effects.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e228.summary: Thomas's determination. From the second way above it follows that God knows not only himself but others. Natural agents tend to ends and must be ordered to them by a knower, which requires knowing the thing, its operation, and its end, as a smith could not make an axe without knowing cutting, what is to be cut, suitable matter, and form to impress. So God must know what is ordered to him, since things have both being and natural order to their end from him (Rabbi Moses reads Ps. 93:9, 'he who formed the eye, does he not see?', this way: in making the eye did he not consider its act, seeing, and its object?). But 'understood', like 'seen', is twofold: the first seen is the species of the visible in the power, the seer's perfection, the principle of vision, and the medium; the second is the thing outside. Likewise the first understood is the likeness in the intellect, the second the thing understood through it. As first understood God understands only himself, since he receives no species but knows by his essence, the likeness of all things; as second understood, he understands others too. The Philosopher's saying that God understands only himself concerns the first sense, and this answers the objections.
claims: God knows other things, since he orders all things to their ends.
God's first object is his essence alone; through it, the likeness of all, he knows others as second objects.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e234.summary: Reply to the first argument. The understood perfects the understander as first understood, not second: the stone outside the soul is not the intellect's perfection, but its likeness in the soul is.
claims: Only the species perfects the intellect.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e237.summary: Reply to the second argument. The divine intellect would be debased by knowing base things if it were informed by their likeness, if it could not understand the noble together with them, or if it understood baser and nobler by different operations. None of these holds; his one operation is most perfect, by which he knows himself and all else.
claims: God's knowledge of base things does not debase it.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e241.summary: Reply to the third argument. That holds for every intellect knowing different things by different species, which God does not, knowing others by knowing his essence.
claims: God knows all by one species, his essence.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e244.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. When many knowables are known by one medium, generic or specific, they reduce to one general or special science, like metaphysics or geometry, and if many are reduced to one medium there is numerically one science of all. So God's knowledge of all things is numerically one, since he knows all by one most simple medium, his essence.
claims: One medium yields one science.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e256.summary: First argument that God lacks certain and proper knowledge of other things. Certain knowledge requires the thing's concept in the knower, and nothing of the same concept is in God and creatures.
claims: No shared concept between God and creatures.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e259.summary: Second argument. A first and remote cause gives no certain knowledge of a thing, and the divine essence is the first and most remote cause.
claims: Remote causes give uncertain knowledge.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e262.summary: Third argument. Proper knowledge is through what is proper to the thing, and one thing cannot be proper to many as many (only as one, like risibility to all men), so knowing all by his one essence God lacks proper knowledge of singulars.
claims: One medium cannot be proper to many.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e266.summary: Fourth argument. What gives certain knowledge of a thing can serve as a middle term to infer it, but the existence of a thing cannot be inferred from the divine essence, since God existed eternally when things did not.
claims: Existence of things does not follow from God's essence.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e269.summary: Sed contra from Metaphysics 1: the knowledge God has is goddess of sciences and most honourable, and he knows things, so most nobly, certainly, and properly.
claims: God's knowledge is the noblest.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e275.summary: Second sed contra. The first in a genus is greatest in it (Metaphysics 2), and knowledge is first in God, so he knows whatever he knows most nobly.
claims: The first is greatest.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e278.summary: Thomas's determination. God knows the proper natures of things most certainly. The Commentator (Metaphysics 2) says God knows other things only as beings: since his being causes the being of all, in knowing it he knows the nature of being found in all, as one knowing fire's heat knows the nature of heat in all hot things but not this or that hot thing as such; nor is God ignorant, since his knowledge is not of our genus, as a stone is neither seeing nor blind. This position is false for two reasons. First, God causes not only things' common being but everything in them: though secondary causes determine each thing to its proper being, all secondary causes are from the first, so whatever is in a thing, proper or common, reduces to God as cause, since of itself a thing has only non-being; so he knows each thing's proper nature. Second, no agent orders its effect to an end without knowing the proper operation by which it is ordered, so if God orders all things to their ends he must know each thing's proper operation and the proper nature suited to it. This holds even if, as some philosophers held, he does not cause order in each thing immediately, a first intelligence proceeding from him, and from it a second intelligence, an orb, and its soul: he must at least know the work of his first creature and so what can be produced through it, and so on down to the last things.
claims: God knows each thing's proper nature, against Averroes' view that he knows things only as beings.
He causes all that is in things, proper or common, and orders each to its end through its proper operation.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e281.summary: Reply to the first argument. Divine being is denied to share the concept of ours not because it falls short but because it exceeds, and the more perfect the medium, the more perfectly a thing is known in it, so as his being exceeds ours, his knowledge of things' being, through his own, exceeds ours, received from things.
claims: God's excelling medium gives more perfect knowledge.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e284.summary: Reply to the second argument. No science is certain except by reduction to its first principles. A first principle in geometry does not suffice for certain knowledge of what follows because it is not their whole cause, so all the others must be added. God is the perfect cause of all that is from him, since nothing can be taken that is not from him, so by his essence he knows all things perfectly.
claims: God, as total cause, knows effects perfectly through himself.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e288.summary: Reply to the third argument. One thing cannot be proper to many that participate it in the same way, wholly and perfectly, but though all things participate divine goodness, none imitates it perfectly, each resembling it in something in which another does not, so God is the proper likeness of each thing, as the one habit of the man with many sciences is the likeness of each of the three habits found in different men, even in what distinguishes them. So one thing can be the proper likeness of many that imitate it imperfectly, as creatures imitate divine goodness.
claims: God's essence is the proper likeness of each thing, since each imitates it imperfectly in its own way.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e291.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Not only divine being causes things to be, but his knowledge and will, from which things' existence is best concluded, since what God wills to be, as he can and knows, comes into being by the power of his essence; these are known to God, so he has certain knowledge of things.
claims: Things' existence follows from God's knowledge and will, which he knows.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e304.summary: First argument that God's knowledge is univocal with ours. An agent by form produces an effect univocal with itself, as fire heat, and God is called wise because he fills us with wisdom by his wisdom (Origen, Dionysius).
claims: Formal agents produce univocal effects.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e307.summary: Second argument. Measure and measured share a concept (dry and wet are measured differently, Metaphysics 3), and God's knowledge measures ours, which is truer the closer it comes.
claims: Measure and measured are of one concept.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e310.summary: Third argument, against excess as a reason for non-univocity. More and less do not diversify species, and excess of knowledge is being more or less knowing.
claims: More and less preserve univocity.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e314.summary: Fourth argument, against the Commentator's reason (God's knowledge causes things, ours is caused by them). Our speculative knowledge is caused by things and practical knowledge causes them, yet 'knowledge' is not equivocal between them.
claims: Causing or being caused does not make equivocity.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e317.summary: Sed contra. The eternal and corruptible share only a name (Commentator and Philosopher, Metaphysics 10), and God's knowledge is eternal, ours corruptible, lost by forgetting and gained by learning.
claims: Eternal and corruptible share only a name.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e320.summary: Second sed contra. Univocal things are alike, and like things are comparable, which requires agreement in a nature, and no creature agrees with God in a common nature, which would be prior to both.
claims: God shares no nature with creatures.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e323.summary: Third sed contra. Nothing univocal is substance in one and accident in another, and knowledge is accident in us, substance in God.
claims: Substance and accident cannot be univocal.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e326.summary: Thomas's determination. Something is common univocally, equivocally, or analogically. Nothing is said univocally of God and creatures: in a thing there is its nature or quiddity and its being, and univocal things share the concept of nature, not being, since one being is only in one thing (humanity is not by the same being in two men). So when the form signified by a name is being itself, it cannot be univocal, which is why 'being' is not predicated univocally. Since the nature or form of whatever is said of God is his being itself, his being being his nature (so some philosophers say he is a being not by essence and knowing not by knowledge, meaning essence is not other than being), nothing is said univocally of God and creatures. Nor purely equivocally, as some hold, since among chance equivocals one is not known from the other, as when two men share a name, while through our knowledge we come to know God's. So knowledge and the like are said analogically. Analogy is twofold: by agreement in some one thing belonging to them by prior and posterior, which cannot hold between God and creature any more than univocity; and by one imitating another as far as it can without fully attaining it, which is the analogy of creature to God.
claims: Nothing is said univocally of God and creatures, since in God the form signified is his very being.
Nor purely equivocally, since we know God from creatures; names are analogical by imitation, not by a shared third.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e329.summary: Reply to the first argument. An agent by form produces a univocal effect only when the recipient can receive the agent's whole power in the same concept, and no creature can receive knowledge from God in the mode it has in him, as lower bodies cannot receive heat univocally from the sun, though it acts by its form.
claims: Univocal effects need proportioned recipients.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e333.summary: Reply to the second argument. God's knowledge is not a measure equal to ours but exceeding it, so it shares its concept not univocally but analogically.
claims: God's knowledge is an exceeding measure.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e336.summary: Reply to the third argument. More and less never remove univocity, but their causes can make specific difference and remove it, when more and less come not from different participation of one nature but from grades of different natures, as an angel is more intellectual than a man.
claims: Grades of different natures remove univocity.
concepts: magis et minus vs. grades of nature

ta-l1d35q1-d1e339.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The Commentator's reason is not sufficient by itself but only as applied to this matter: knowledge that causes things as divine knowledge does cannot be univocal with knowledge caused by things, for the reason given.
claims: Causing as God causes excludes univocity.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e342.summary: Reply to the first sed contra, since the contrary arguments seem to conclude pure equivocity. The saying concerns being, not the intention commonly predicated: even 'body' is said equivocally of corruptible and incorruptible things in that sense, though its concept is the same in both by common intention.
claims: Eternal and corruptible differ in being, not necessarily in common intention.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e345.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Between God and creature there is likeness not by agreement in something common but by imitation, so the creature is called like God, but not conversely (Dionysius).
claims: Creatures are like God, not God like creatures.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e348.summary: Reply to the third sed contra. Knowledge is predicated of God not by its genus, accidental quality, but only by its difference, which pertains to perfection, in which nature is attended by imitation.
claims: Knowledge is said of God by its perfecting difference, not its genus.
concepts: genus vs. difference in divine predication

ta-l1d35q1-d1e360.summary: First argument that God's knowledge is universal. Universal knowledge is through universal causes, and God knows all by the most universal cause, his essence.
claims: God knows by the most universal cause.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e363.summary: Second argument that it is particular. Particular knowledge knows a thing's proper nature, which God knows perfectly.
claims: God knows proper natures.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e366.summary: Third argument that it is potential. As God's operation extends to things outside, so does his knowledge, and he did not always actually produce things, so he is not always actually knowing.
claims: Knowledge parallels operation.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e370.summary: Fourth argument that it is habitual. As power is between essence and operation, habit is between power and act, and we distinguish essence, operation, and power in God, so we may say he is knowing habitually.
claims: Habit between power and act.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e373.summary: Fifth argument that it is actual. Nothing acts except as in act, and God makes all things by wisdom (Ps. 103:24).
claims: God acts by wisdom, so it is actual.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e379.summary: Sed contra. Things not of the same concept are not divided by the same differences, and God's knowledge and ours are not of the same concept.
claims: Our knowledge's differences do not apply to God's.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e382.summary: Second sed contra. The Commentator says God's knowledge is neither universal, nor particular, nor potential.
claims: Averroes denies these of God's knowledge.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e385.summary: Thomas's determination. None of these fits divine knowledge except being always in act, since the conditions of knowledge follow chiefly the medium, and God's medium is his essence. It is not universal, since every universal receives an addition by which it is determined and so is potential and imperfect in being; nor particular, since the principle of particularity is matter or something in its place, which does not fit God; nor potential, since all passive or material potency is removed from him as pure act; nor habitual, since a habit is not the ultimate perfection, which is rather the operation perfecting it. So his knowledge is only actual.
claims: God's knowledge is neither universal, particular, potential, nor habitual, but only actual, since its medium is his essence.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e388.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though the divine essence is the universal cause of things, nothing is added to it to make it a proper and perfect cause; it is by itself the sufficient, perfect cause of each thing, so knowledge through it is not universal but of each thing's proper nature.
claims: God's essence is a sufficient proper cause of each thing.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e392.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though God knows each thing's proper nature, he does not know it by anything received from the thing, since divine knowledge does not insert itself into singulars (Dionysius), nor knows himself and others by different knowledge, so it is not particular, which properly is knowledge through a particular medium received from the thing.
claims: God's knowledge of singulars is not received from them.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e395.summary: Reply to the third argument. God does not act by a mediating operation; his operation is his essence, so like his knowledge it is always in act, though its product is not always, by the order of his disposing wisdom. Yet God is not said to have made things eternally as he knew them eternally, since operation is signified as going from operator to product, so God is called making only when something is made; but knowing, though of external things, concerns them only as they are in the knower by their likeness, so by the condition of the knower, not the known, God is said to have known eternally even what was not eternal.
claims: God's operation is always in act; its effects are temporal.
God knew eternally what was not eternal, by the condition of the knower.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e398.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Power (virtus) names a perfect principle of operation, so we can signify operative power in God, but a habit is only the perfection of a power incomplete for act, and not the ultimate, so it implies a double imperfection, in the power perfected by habit and in the habit perfected by operation. So 'habit' does not properly fit God, and if God is sometimes said to be Lord eternally 'in habit', not act, it is by likeness rather than propriety.
claims: 'Habitus' does not properly fit God, implying double imperfection.

ta-l1d35q1-d1e407.summary: An expositio textus. (1) Of the names of God's one knowledge, each adds to the other not on the side of the knower but of the known, which relate to knowledge differently: 'knowledge' or 'wisdom' says cognition with certainty, of temporal and eternal things; 'foreknowledge' adds duration, eternity to time, so it concerns only temporal things, good and evil; 'disposition' adds the order of cause to effect in being, so it concerns things to be made; 'providence' adds the order of a cause conserving and ordering to an end, so it belongs to governance; 'predestination' adds a determinate end, so it concerns only those ordered to glory, the good to be saved; 'reprobation', of evils, adds nothing pertaining to knowledge beyond foreknowledge, so it is not mentioned here. (2) The three objections proceed alike from foreknowledge signified abstractly, verbally ('to foreknow'), and concretely non-neutrally ('foreknowing'). (3) 'Creator is said relatively so as not to signify the essence' seems false, since as a verbal noun it signifies an act, and the act of creation in God is the essence; but creation as divine action includes the operation, which is the essence, and the relation to the creature, and Lombard takes 'Creator' as imposed from the relation, which is not the essence nor anything real in God.
claims: The names of divine knowledge add conditions on the side of the objects.
'Creator' taken from the relation does not signify the essence.

ta-l1d35q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 35 divides the treatment of God as voluntary principle into knowledge, power, and will (Dist. 35–48) and Lombard's account of the various names of God's one knowledge. It announces five articles on God's knowledge: its existence, its extension to others, its certainty and propriety, its analogy with ours, and its mode.
claims: God's knowledge, power, and will complete his character as principle.

ta-l1d35q1-Dd1e139.summary: Article 1 holds that God has knowledge, by Dionysius's three ways: removal (immaterial subsistent form is intelligent), causality (the first agent directs nature to ends by intellect), and eminence (degrees of knowledge culminate in God). Names like 'knowing' are said properly of God as to the thing signified, not as mere negation or likeness of effect. They are one in reality and conceptually distinct, as one habit may contain many sciences. Knower and known are one in act, and in God, pure act, they differ only conceptually; receptive vocabulary belongs to the possible intellect, and discursus is removed from divine knowledge.
claims: God is knowing by the ways of removal, causality, and eminence.
Divine names are said properly as to the thing signified; in God knower, known, and knowledge are one.

ta-l1d35q1-Dd1e198.summary: Article 2 holds that God knows things other than himself, since he orders all things to their ends. His first object is his essence alone, and through it, the likeness of all things, he knows others as second objects. This does not debase or multiply his knowledge, since he knows all by one operation and one medium.
claims: God knows others through his essence as their likeness.
His knowledge of all is one.

ta-l1d35q1-Dd1e248.summary: Article 3 holds, against Averroes, that God knows each thing's proper nature with certainty. He causes all that is in things, proper or common, and orders each to its end through its proper operation. His excelling medium, as total cause, gives more perfect knowledge, his essence is the proper likeness of each thing imperfectly imitating it, and things' existence follows from his known will.
claims: God knows the proper natures of all things, against Averroes.

ta-l1d35q1-Dd1e296.summary: Article 4 holds that knowledge is said of God and creatures neither univocally, since in God the form signified is his being, which is not shared, nor purely equivocally, since we know God's knowledge from ours, but analogically, by imitation, not by agreement in a common third. Univocal effects need proportioned recipients, God's knowledge is an exceeding measure, grades of nature remove univocity, and knowledge is said of God by its perfecting difference, not its genus.
claims: Knowledge is analogical between God and creatures, by imitation.

ta-l1d35q1-Dd1e352.summary: Article 5 holds that God's knowledge is neither universal, particular, potential, nor habitual, but only actual, since its medium is his essence, a sufficient proper cause of each thing, not received from things. His operation is always in act though its effects are temporal, and he knew eternally what was not eternal.
claims: God's knowledge is only actual.

ta-l1d35q1-Dd1e402.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 35 orders the names of God's knowledge (knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, providence, predestination) by the conditions they add on the side of the objects. It explains that 'Creator', taken from the relation, does not signify the essence.
claims: The names of divine knowledge add conditions from their objects.

ta-l1d35q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 35 treats God's knowledge. Article 1 holds that God is knowing by the ways of removal, causality, and eminence, with knower, known, and knowledge one in him, and that such names are said properly as to the thing signified. Article 2 holds that he knows other things through his essence, their likeness. Article 3 holds, against Averroes, that he knows the proper nature of each thing, as total cause and orderer. Article 4 holds that knowledge is analogical between God and creatures, by imitation. Article 5 holds that his knowledge is only actual, not universal, particular, potential, or habitual.
claims: God knows himself and all things through his essence, properly and with certainty.
Knowledge is analogical between God and creatures.
God's knowledge is pure act.
